title: OBR on the Budget: energy shock, weak productivity and tight fiscal headroom
label: 4 November 2026 · Treasury Committee session with the OBR
summary: The Office for Budget Responsibility explained why the Budget outlook reflects a short-lived energy shock, a modest medium‑term recovery, and persistently weak living standards driven by low productivity, energy costs and higher effective taxes. The OBR stressed many Budget measures remain unspecified so uncertainty is high, judged the fiscal headroom (£15bn) as small (about a 56% chance of sufficiency), and flagged risks from migration, welfare, temporary tax cuts and enforcement-based revenue claims.

Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that produces the UK's official economic and fiscal forecasts.
The OBR's economic and fiscal outlook report published on Budget day.

chapters.title: Independence and purpose
chapters.takeaway: The OBR confirms it acted independently and produced the required Budget forecast (the Blue Book).

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Professor Haskel, can you confirm you faced no political pressure when preparing the economic and fiscal outlook?

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: Yes—I can confirm there was no undue pressure from Ministers or the Treasury in producing the forecast.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: You downgraded growth for this year and next, but then project a recovery—what assumptions drive that profile?

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: The near-term downgrade is largely the energy-price shock; we use market (futures) prices which imply a temporary hit, then a recovery as prices fall back, plus modestly higher investment and some AI-driven productivity later on.

chapters.title: Energy shock and the growth path
chapters.takeaway: High energy prices are the main reason growth is weaker now and into next year; the OBR treats that as a temporary interruption but flags big uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Professor David Miles
turns.text: Markets are pricing much higher oil and gas for the near term—gas is about three times what it was early in the year—so we expect a squeeze on incomes and higher inflation into early next year.

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: In our models a large energy shock temporarily reduces firm capital productivity; when market prices fall again, growth returns toward medium-term potential.

turns.speaker: Seema Malhotra
turns.text: Do markets already price in the Middle East risks, and could that make your outlook too pessimistic or optimistic?

turns.speaker: Professor David Miles
turns.text: The futures curve is the central market view; it could go either way—if prices fall faster we'd forecast lower inflation and stronger growth; if prices stay high, the downside worsens.

turns.speaker: Ms Minns
turns.text: You assume the energy-price cap peaks early next year—if it ends up £300 higher, does that undo your policy impact on inflation?

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: Not automatically. The cap depends partly on wholesale prices and other components; we used the futures curve. A higher cap raises uncertainty but doesn't immediately invalidate the forecast.

chapters.title: Why living standards look weak
chapters.takeaway: The OBR expects very low real household income growth this decade, driven mainly by persistently weak productivity, energy shocks and rising effective taxes.

turns.speaker: Bobby Dean
turns.text: Your chart shows real household disposable income growth this decade at about 1.4%—what keeps it so low when energy prices unwind?

turns.speaker: Professor David Miles
turns.text: Three factors: very weak productivity growth since the financial crisis, the current energy shock, and a higher average tax take driven by frozen tax thresholds pushing people into higher bands.

turns.speaker: Bobby Dean
turns.text: Could policy or luck lift the decade back to the 2010s level (14%)?

turns.speaker: Professor David Miles
turns.text: That would need a lot of good luck—sharp falls in energy prices and major productivity gains, for example from rapid AI-driven adoption; it's possible but unlikely in our central view.

turns.speaker: Seema Malhotra
turns.text: You assume AI lifts annual productivity by about 0.2 percentage points—what evidence supports that magnitude?

turns.speaker: Professor David Miles
turns.text: Economists disagree widely: some foresee near-zero impact, others a transformative boost. We took a cautious, modest contribution; if AI is transformative, the fiscal upside would be large.

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: Sector data helps: ICT services showed very strong productivity recently (about 7.6% over two years), which looks linked to AI; how far that spreads to other sectors determines the economy-wide gain.

chapters.title: Scoring policies and key uncertainties
chapters.takeaway: Many Budget measures are high-level or temporary, so the OBR treated them cautiously; several announced changes arrived after the forecast and will be assessed later.

turns.speaker: Dame Harriett Baldwin
turns.text: You flagged that higher tax on landlords could raise rents; can you quantify that effect?

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: We haven't produced a precise number yet—pass-through depends on supply-demand and substitution between renting and owning, so we need more work.

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: Some policy announcements arrived after our forecast—like the Government's ILR decision on migrants—so we didn't include them; we'll reassess in the spring forecast if material.

turns.speaker: Dame Harriett Baldwin
turns.text: You scored the Employment Rights Act as negative for growth but below your materiality threshold—how big is that threshold?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: Our threshold for a quantifiable productivity effect is 0.1% of GDP. We judged the ERA would raise business costs but were too uncertain to say it exceeded that threshold.

turns.speaker: Ms Minns
turns.text: You flagged temporary measures (VAT cut, fuel duty) as risks—if those are extended, you'll change the forecast?

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: Yes. We follow announced government policy for the central forecast; if the Government extends temporary cuts, we would update and flag the fiscal risk.

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: On fuel duty specifically: it hasn't risen since 2011. If it stays frozen, we estimate borrowing would be about £4bn a year higher than if uprated.

chapters.title: Headroom, debt costs and spending pressures
chapters.takeaway: The Chancellor set £15bn headroom—OBR estimates about a 55–56% chance that is sufficient, and many policy and spending risks remain, including welfare and departmental efficiency targets.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: Is £15bn headroom realistic given typical forecast revisions? Will it be used before the next fiscal event?

turns.speaker: Professor David Miles
turns.text: Headroom at £15bn gives roughly a 55–56% chance of staying positive in three years—better than a coin toss but not a comfortable margin. Revisions swing both ways.

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: To reach a 60% chance you'd need about £25bn, and for a 70% chance roughly £50bn—so the chosen number is modest relative to uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Andrew Lewin
turns.text: You include a Rosebank assumption—how material is a single field to oil and gas receipts?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: Our production path follows the North Sea Transition Authority field-by-field projections. Revenues are declining overall; all fields together are projected to generate only a few hundred million in the long run.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: You forecast unprotected departmental resource spending falling sharply—has such a fall ever been delivered?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: Governments can and have reduced spending as a share of GDP. The projection reflects choices needed to meet commitments (defence, health, education) and efficiency targets; the next spending review will clarify what's assumed.

turns.speaker: Dame Harriett Baldwin
turns.text: Welfare is a big unknown—you raised your baseline by £5bn a year and say risks could push it £25bn higher; will the Government's planned employment programmes be reflected in your numbers?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: We only score policies when there are final details and delivery funding. Past experience shows programs often change on delivery, so we need concrete plans before altering forecasts.

chapters.title: Tax measures, compliance and smaller items
chapters.takeaway: Some announced tax changes are small in macro terms but uncertain (founders' relief, bank surcharge, HMRC compliance); enforcement gains are plausible but hard to rely on fully.

turns.speaker: Dame Harriett Baldwin
turns.text: The bank surcharge raises about £1.5bn—did you judge moving capital into state-backed banks is more or less productive than private use?

turns.speaker: Professor Jonathan Haskel
turns.text: We treated the measure as a revenue/transfers exercise; we didn't assume any large effect on productive capital. We did estimate only a small potential impact on bank lending and flagged about £190m of profit shifting risk overseas.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Founders' relief was debated—did you model behavioural responses or growth effects?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: Founders' relief is small in our forecast (around £200m) so we didn't do a detailed macro assessment; we cost it fiscally but did not assume large economic effects.

turns.speaker: Dame Harriett Baldwin
turns.text: HMRC compliance measures claim about £3bn of extra receipts—how realistic is that?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: We treat compliance gains cautiously. We model them and work with HMRC, but such estimates are uncertain because taxpayers and firms may change behaviour or shift tax positions. The fiscal gap could fall to historically achieved levels, but there is upside and downside risk.

turns.speaker: Bobby Dean
turns.text: Capital spending underspend was lower than expected—was that faster project delivery, inflation, or both?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: We assess capital spending top-down and haven't traced each project. Likely a mix of faster delivery and higher costs; departments appear to have spent more of their capital envelopes than we previously expected.

turns.speaker: Jim Dickson
turns.text: On devolution, you say it's too early to score—what final details would you need?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: We'd need firm rates, how much funding is devolved, and any revenue equalisation arrangements—outcomes also depend strongly on local delivery capacity, so even with details the impacts can be hard to predict.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you—final practical question: will you publish changes arising from late policy tweaks made just before Budget day?

turns.speaker: Tom Josephs
turns.text: We record and disclose late changes. A couple of small parameter tweaks were made to fuel duty and two other measures; we will follow up in writing with the specific items and the size of the impact.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thanks to the OBR members—Professor Haskel, Professor Miles and Tom Josephs—for a clear account of where the forecast rests and where the big uncertainties lie.
